baseline.name: Chinook Salmon
baseline.description: The largest Pacific salmon, with robust silver body and black spots on upper back and BOTH lobes of tail. Adults develop hooked jaw (kype). Black gum line is the key ID marker.
baseline.season: Spring Chinook: Apr-Jun in Columbia. Fall Chinook: Aug-Oct. Ocean: May-Sept offshore.
gpsHints: Buoy 10 at the Columbia River mouth — launch from East Mooring Basin Astoria
Youngs Bay off of Hwy 202
baseline.regulations: Combined Angling Tag required. Hatchery only (clipped adipose fin) for retention in most areas. Check ODFW for current limits.

tackle.technique: Back-troll Kwikfish or plug-cut herring in the Columbia. Anchor and plunk egg clusters in side channels. Troll hoochies/flashers offshore.

funFacts: Can weigh over 100 lbs and live up to 8 years
Travels hundreds of miles upriver to spawn in the same gravel bed it was born in
The Columbia River once produced the largest Chinook runs in the world
baseline.memoryHook: KING-sized fish: black gum line, black spots on BOTH tail lobes — the KING rules all salmon
identifyingFeatures: Black spots on both lobes of tail fin
Irregularly shaped black spots on back

baseline.name: Coho Salmon
baseline.description: Bright silver ocean fish with small black spots only on the UPPER lobe of the tail. White gums with black tip on tongue. Aggressive strikers make them favorites.
baseline.season: Ocean: Aug-Oct. Columbia River: Sept-Nov. Necanicum/Nehalem: Oct-Dec.
gpsHints: Necanicum River — Hwy 101 bridge in Seaside is a classic bank spot
Charter boats from Warrenton Marina for ocean Coho
baseline.regulations: Combined Angling Tag required. Hatchery only (check adipose fin clip). Bag limit typically 2/day in river.

tackle.technique: Cast and retrieve spinners across current in rivers. Troll spinners or hoochies behind a flasher offshore at 2-3 mph. Drift eggs under a float.

funFacts: Coho are famous for spectacular aerial leaps when hooked
They return to spawn at exactly 3 years old
White-fleshed coho are sometimes called "silvers" — the silver color comes from ocean feeding
baseline.memoryHook: Silver Salmon = spots on UPPER tail lobe only. White gums with black tip. COHOerent color (all silver).
identifyingFeatures: White gums with black tip on tongue
Spots only on upper lobe of tail
Small black spots on back (not both tail lobes)

baseline.name: Lingcod
baseline.description: Large, mottled green-brown predator with huge mouth full of teeth. One of the ocean's apex predators — will eat other fish right off your hook. Blue-green flesh (edible, turns white when cooked).
baseline.season: Open most of year offshore. Peak Oct-Mar for nearshore, summer for deeper water.
gpsHints: Charter boats from Warrenton Marina run to nearshore reefs
Tillamook Head reefs — boat access only
baseline.regulations: Minimum 22 inches (check current ODFW). Bag limit 2/day. No retention during certain spawning periods.

tackle.technique: Jig heavy metal or soft plastics near rocky bottom. Let jig hit bottom, rip up 4-5 feet, drop back. Often holds just above structure. Will grab rockfish off hook.

funFacts: Lingcod flesh is naturally blue-green but turns white when cooked — perfectly edible
Males guard eggs for weeks after spawning
Can live to 20+ years and grow to 5 feet
baseline.memoryHook: LING-cOD: Big head, big teeth, LING-ers near the bottom. Blue flesh = distinctive ID.
identifyingFeatures: Very large mouth with many teeth

baseline.name: Pacific Halibut
baseline.description: Massive flatfish, dark brown on top and white underneath. Both eyes on the same side of the head (right side). Can exceed 200 lbs. Prized table fare — firm white flesh.
baseline.season: Oregon halibut season typically May-Sept (check ODFW each year). Peak June-Aug.
gpsHints: Charter boats from East Mooring Basin Astoria — all-day trips to offshore grounds
baseline.regulations: 1 per day, minimum size varies. Check ODFW for current season dates — season can close early if quota is reached.

lures: Whole herring or smelt (drift or anchor)
Large spreader bar rigs with herring
tackle.technique: Drift across sandy bottom at correct depth. Circle hook with whole herring on a spreader bar rig. Let bait sit on bottom, sweep rod, wait for weight of fish. Never yank on circle hooks.

funFacts: Both eyes migrate to the right side of the head as the fish grows from larval form
Halibut can live over 55 years
A single halibut can provide over 100 lbs of white fillets
baseline.memoryHook: HALI-but (HALE and able): BOTH eyes on right side. FLAT, dark on top, white below.
identifyingFeatures: Both eyes on right side of head
Lateral line with distinct curve over pectoral fin

baseline.name: Black Rockfish
baseline.description: Dark gray to black schooling rockfish. Large eyes, spiny dorsal fin with mild venom. Found in mid-water column near rocky structure. Highly prized sportfish.
baseline.season: Open most of year. Best May-Oct from charter or private boat.
gpsHints: Haystack Rock visible from Cannon Beach — rockfish in the kelp zone around it (boat required)
baseline.regulations: Bag limit check ODFW. Typically 10 combined rockfish per day. Avoid crushing barotrauma fish — use descender device.

tackle.technique: Drift over rocky reefs, jig vertically or cast and count down. Mid-water column schools. Light jigs work great — these fish are aggressive biters.

funFacts: Rockfish can live 50-100+ years — a "small" fish may be older than you
Black rockfish school in midwater unlike many other rockfish
Mild venom in spines — handle with care
baseline.memoryHook: BLACK rockfish = black coloring, MID-water column, schools near rocky reefs.
identifyingFeatures: Found in schools mid-water near rocks

baseline.name: Cabezon
baseline.description: Bizarre-looking large sculpin with mottled red-brown coloring, huge pectoral fins, and a flap of skin (cirrus) above each eye. Found on rocky bottom. Eggs are toxic — do not eat the roe.
baseline.season: Good year-round. Best Oct-Mar nearshore. Spawning Jan-Mar.
gpsHints: South Jetty at Fort Stevens State Park — accessible from parking area off Ridge Road
baseline.regulations: 10 per day (combined with other sculpin). No size limit typically.

tackle.technique: Fish on bottom near rocks. Cabezon are ambush predators — use realistic crab/shrimp imitations. Be patient. No need for long casts — fish right among the rocks.

funFacts: Cabezon eggs are poisonous — bright red or green depending on diet, NEVER eat the roe
Males guard the egg mass until it hatches
They can change color to match their surroundings
baseline.memoryHook: CABezon = Crazy Appearance Beast. Blob-like, fleshy cirrus above eyes, EGGS ARE TOXIC.
identifyingFeatures: Large fleshy flap (cirrus) above each eye

baseline.name: Redtail Surfperch
baseline.description: Silvery perch with distinctive reddish-orange tail and fin edges. The premier target for surf anglers along Oregon beaches. Livebearers — give birth to fully formed young.
baseline.season: Year-round but best Feb-May (pre-spawn). Good Sept-Nov. Summer low period.
gpsHints: Del Rey Beach — park at the end of Del Rey Beach Rd, walk north along the beach
Fort Stevens Beach — drive-on beach near Peter Iredale wreck
baseline.regulations: 15 per day, no size limit. No license required for surfperch from the beach in Oregon.

tackle.technique: Fish 1-3 waves out in the surf zone. Sand shrimp under a 1-2oz pyramid sinker. Cast into troughs between sandbars. Incoming tide 2hrs before to 2hrs after high is best.

funFacts: Surfperch give birth to live young — no eggs
They feed in the turbulent surf zone where other fish cannot survive
No fishing license needed to target them from the beach in Oregon
baseline.memoryHook: REDTAIL: red/orange fins, SURF zone, needs NO LICENSE from beach. Oregon's most accessible fish.

baseline.name: Albacore Tuna
baseline.description: Fast, streamlined tuna with extremely long pectoral fins (longer than any other tuna). Steel-blue back, silver belly. Warm-blooded and capable of incredible speeds. Best eating of all Pacific tuna.
baseline.season: August-October offshore, 40-80 miles out. Depends on warm water (60°F+).
gpsHints: East Mooring Basin Astoria — charter boats for albacore troll trips August-October
baseline.regulations: 25 per person per day. Ocean boat license required.

tackle.rod: 6-7ft heavy trolling rod or stand-up conventional
tackle.technique: Troll at 6-9 knots using cedar plugs and feathers on long lines (40-80ft back). When fish are found, stop boat and cast jigs. Watch for birds and temperature breaks.

funFacts: Albacore can swim up to 50 mph in short bursts
They are warm-blooded, maintaining body temperature above ocean temperature
Pacific albacore from Oregon are considered the best tuna for canning
baseline.memoryHook: ALBACORE = LONG pectoral fins (longer than body depth). WAY offshore. Expensive charter but worth it.
identifyingFeatures: Extremely long pectoral fins (reaches past anal fin)

baseline.name: White Sturgeon
baseline.description: North America's largest freshwater fish — prehistoric dinosaur-like fish with rows of bony plates (scutes) instead of scales. Can live 100+ years and grow to 20 feet. Found in the Columbia River.
baseline.season: Year-round in Columbia River. Retainable seasons vary — check ODFW. Best Sept-April.
gpsHints: Tongue Point near Astoria — anchor in the channel during incoming tide
East Mooring Basin Astoria — boat launch for Columbia River access
baseline.regulations: SLOT LIMIT: Must be 44-50 inches fork length to retain (Columbia River). Release over/undersized fish carefully. Requires Combined Angling Tag.

tackle.reel: Large conventional (Penn 320 GTi or similar) 30lb+ drag
tackle.technique: Anchor and bottom-fish with a 3-way swivel rig. Heavy pyramid or slinky sinker. Use circle hooks 7/0-10/0. DO NOT set hook — let circle hook do the work. Very slow, patient game.

funFacts: White sturgeon are living fossils — their body plan has remained unchanged for 200 million years
A single large female may contain over 100 lbs of caviar (roe)
They can live to 100+ years — some Columbia River fish were alive during the Civil War
baseline.memoryHook: STURGEON = PREHISTORIC rows of bony scutes (not scales). Columbia River GIANT. Slot limit — measure before keeping.
identifyingFeatures: Rows of bony scutes (plates) along body

baseline.name: Winter Steelhead
baseline.description: Sea-run rainbow trout — the most coveted freshwater gamefish in the Pacific Northwest. Chrome-bright from the ocean, gaining color as they enter freshwater. Fight much harder than resident rainbows.
baseline.season: Dec-March (peak Jan-Feb) on local rivers. Some summer steelhead in warmer months.
gpsHints: Necanicum River — US 101 pullouts near Seaside, or below Necanicum Hatchery
Klaskanine River — off Hwy 202 east of Astoria, multiple access points
baseline.regulations: Combined Angling Tag required. Hatchery fish (clipped adipose) only for retention on most local rivers. Wild steelhead release only.

tackle.rod: 8.5-10ft medium-heavy drift rod or switch rod
tackle.reel: Large capacity spinning or centerpin reel
tackle.line: 15-20lb mono or 30lb braid with 10-15lb fluoro leader
tackle.technique: Drift fishing: float (bobber) with jig, eggs, or shrimp. Or swing flies in the traditional style. Fish seam between fast and slow water. Early mornings after rain events = best conditions.

funFacts: Steelhead are genetically identical to rainbow trout but spend part of their life at sea
A steelhead may make multiple spawning trips — unlike Pacific salmon they survive spawning
Winter steelhead can be found in rivers within days of ocean entry
baseline.memoryHook: STEELHEAD = CHROME (ocean fresh), then picks up pink stripe as they color up in the river. Sea-run RAINBOW.
identifyingFeatures: Distinct pink lateral stripe (fresh run fish less colored)
Black spots on body and fins
Larger, more muscular than resident rainbow trout

baseline.name: Sea-run Cutthroat Trout
baseline.description: Native trout with distinctive red-orange "slash" marks under the jaw. Sea-run fish return from estuaries bright silver. A beloved Oregon treasure found in small coastal streams.
baseline.season: Sept-Nov in rivers (best Sept-Oct). Year-round in estuaries. Summer in lakes.
gpsHints: Necanicum River — walk the banks in Seaside near the Broadway Bridge for sea-run cutthroat in October
baseline.regulations: Check ODFW. Often catch-and-release on specific streams. No retention of wild fish in many coastal rivers.

tackle.line: 6-10lb mono or fluoro, or 5-6wt fly line
tackle.technique: Work upstream, cast spinners across and slightly upstream, retrieve through pools and runs. On fly, swing a Woolly Bugger through the pool. Very spooky fish — stay low and cast carefully.

funFacts: The "cutthroat" name comes from the red slash marks under the jaw
Sea-run cutthroat shuttle between ocean and freshwater without dying like Pacific salmon
They feed heavily on salmon eggs during spawning season
baseline.memoryHook: CUTthroat = RED slashes under jaw like a cut. SEA-RUN fish go silver but always keep the slashes.
identifyingFeatures: Red-orange slash marks under jaw (always present)
Black spots throughout body including belly
Sea-run fish bright silver, resident fish yellowish
Spots all the way to tail fin

baseline.name: American Shad
baseline.description: Silvery, deep-bodied herring-like fish with a row of dark spots along the lateral line. Introduced to the Columbia River in 1871. Massive spring runs. Great sport fish — fights hard for its size.
baseline.season: May-July in the Columbia River. Peak late May to mid-June.
locations: Columbia River near Astoria and Tongue Point
gpsHints: Tongue Point area near Astoria — excellent bank access during the May-June run
baseline.regulations: 25 per day on Columbia River. Combined angling license required.

tackle.line: 8-12lb mono or 20lb braid with 8lb fluoro leader
tackle.technique: Cast across current and let drift/swing. Use very light jigs. Shad dart or small spinner in current seams. Pound per pound one of the hardest fighting fish in fresh water.

funFacts: American shad were introduced to the Pacific Coast in 1871 and have thrived ever since
Their roe is considered a delicacy — shad roe is a traditional spring dish on the East Coast
A single female may carry 30,000 eggs
baseline.memoryHook: SHAD = row of spots along side, DEEP body like a herring. MAY-JUNE Columbia run. Dart or spinner.
identifyingFeatures: Row of dark spots behind the gill cover

baseline.name: Walleye
baseline.description: Long, torpedo-shaped fish with distinctive milky, cloudy (glass) eyes due to a reflective layer (tapetum lucidum) that gives excellent night vision. Olive-gold coloring with white-tipped lower tail lobe.
baseline.season: Year-round in Columbia River. Best Apr-Jun and Oct-Dec. Dawn and dusk feeding.
gpsHints: Columbia River — walleye prefer sandy/gravelly bottom in the mid-to-upper Columbia, less common near Astoria
baseline.regulations: 5 per day on Columbia River. No size limit in most Columbia sections.

tackle.line: 10-17lb fluoro or 20-30lb braid with 10lb fluoro leader
tackle.technique: Troll Rapala Shad Rap near bottom at 1.5-2 mph. Or drift Lindy rigs with nightcrawlers. Fish low-light periods — walleye have exceptional night vision. Jig vertically over rocky humps.

funFacts: Walleye eyes have a tapetum lucidum (reflective layer) that makes them glow in the dark like cats
They are primarily crepuscular — most active at dawn, dusk, and night
Walleye are considered the best-tasting freshwater fish by many anglers
baseline.memoryHook: WALLeye = glassy, milky EYES (tapetum lucidum). GOLD/olive coloring. White tip on lower tail. Night hunter.
identifyingFeatures: White tip on bottom lobe of tail fin

baseline.name: Smallmouth Bass
baseline.description: Bronzy-green bass with vertical bars on the sides. Upper jaw does NOT extend past the eye (smaller mouth than largemouth). Pound for pound considered one of the toughest fighters in freshwater.
baseline.season: May-September in Columbia and Youngs River. Peak June-August.
gpsHints: Columbia River — gravel bars downstream of Astoria. Rocky structure areas near islands.
baseline.regulations: No size limit or bag limit in Columbia River. Check ODFW for specific waters.

tackle.line: 8-15lb fluoro or 20-30lb braid with 10-12lb fluoro leader
tackle.technique: Target rocky banks, gravel bars, and submerged structure. Drag a tube jig slowly along bottom. In rivers, cast upstream of rocks and let lure tumble naturally past.

funFacts: Smallmouth bass are said to fight 3x harder than largemouth for their size
They prefer cooler, cleaner water than largemouth and are an indicator of water quality
Male smallmouth guard the nest and fry aggressively after spawning
baseline.memoryHook: SMALL mouth = jaw does NOT extend past eye. BRONZE coloring with vertical bars. Rocky water fighter.
identifyingFeatures: Upper jaw ends at or before the eye (key difference from largemouth)

baseline.name: Rainbow Trout
baseline.description: The classic hatchery trout — silvery with pink lateral stripe and black spots. ODFW stocks many Clatsop County lakes. Freshwater cousin of steelhead — same species, just different life history.
baseline.season: Year-round in stocked lakes. ODFW plants heavily spring (Apr-May) and fall (Sept-Oct).
gpsHints: Coffenbury Lake — parking lot at Fort Stevens State Park off Ridge Road
Cullaby Lake — boat ramp on Cullaby Lake Rd off Hwy 101
baseline.regulations: 5 per day, 8-inch minimum (check ODFW for specific lakes). Some waters are catch-and-release.

tackle.technique: From shore: PowerBait on a sliding sinker rig, no float — let dough float just off bottom. From boat: troll Kastmaster or Rapala at 2 mph. Hatchery fish respond well to scented baits.

funFacts: Hatchery rainbow trout are descended from wild fish from Shasta River, CA — all Pacific NW hatchery fish trace back to the same brood stock
They can be caught within hours of stocking
Rainbow and steelhead are the same species — Oncorhynchus mykiss
baseline.memoryHook: RAINBOW = pink lateral stripe + black spots. STOCKED in local lakes. PowerBait = instant trout magnet.
identifyingFeatures: Black spots on body, dorsal fin, and tail
Smaller adipose fin (may be clipped in hatchery fish)

baseline.name: Largemouth Bass
baseline.description: America's most popular gamefish. Olive-green with dark lateral stripe from head to tail. Upper jaw extends past the eye (KEY difference from smallmouth). Ambush predator in weedy, warm lakes.
baseline.season: Year-round. Spawning May-June. Best May-Sept in Clatsop County lakes.
gpsHints: Cullaby Lake — boat ramp on Cullaby Lake Rd. Fish the weed beds in the eastern coves
Smith Lake — off US 101 near Warrenton, county park access
baseline.regulations: No size or bag limit in most Oregon waters (check local regs). Tournaments subject to rules.

tackle.line: 14-20lb fluoro or 40-65lb braid with 12-16lb fluoro leader
tackle.technique: Cast into weeds/structure with Texas-rigged soft plastic. Slow down — largemouth are ambush feeders. Frog on lily pads at dawn is phenomenal. Spinnerbait retrieved through grass pockets.

funFacts: Largemouth bass can inhale and exhale water in milliseconds to create suction that pulls prey in
They are one of the most studied fish species in the world due to bass fishing's popularity
Female largemouth grow larger than males — a 10+ lb bass is always a female
baseline.memoryHook: LARGEmouth = jaw goes PAST the eye. DARK lateral stripe head-to-tail. Loves lily pads and weeds.
identifyingFeatures: Upper jaw extends clearly past the rear of the eye
Horizontal dark stripe along lateral line
Notch between front spiny and rear soft dorsal fin

baseline.name: Yellow Perch
baseline.description: Vividly colored small fish with yellow-green body, 6-8 dark vertical bars, and orange-red lower fins. School in large numbers. Excellent eating — sweet, white, flaky flesh.
baseline.season: Year-round. Best Oct-April (winter schools at depth). Summer in deeper water.
gpsHints: Cullaby Lake — fish 8-15ft depth near submerged structure and dock areas
baseline.regulations: 25 per day, no size limit in Oregon.

tackle.technique: Fish vertically in schools using small jigs or live bait. Locate school with electronics or by watching for perch dimpling the surface. When you catch one, stay — the whole school is there.

funFacts: Yellow perch is considered one of the best-tasting freshwater fish in North America
They school in large groups — once you find one, you've found hundreds
Perch are highly social — if you catch one from a school and throw it back, it leads others away
baseline.memoryHook: YELLOW with BARS (like a football jersey). Orange-red lower fins. Schools = keep fishing same spot.
identifyingFeatures: 6-8 dark vertical bars on yellow-green body

baseline.name: Bluegill
baseline.description: Colorful sunfish with blue-purple opercular flap (earflap), olive-yellow body with dark vertical bars, and orange-yellow belly. The classic pond fish — perfect for beginning anglers.
baseline.season: Year-round. Best April-September. Spawning May-July in shallow water.
gpsHints: Coffenbury Lake — fish the shallow, weedy southern cove from shore or canoe
baseline.regulations: 25 per day, no size limit in Oregon.

lures: Small red worm/nightcrawler piece on #8-10 hook
Fly: small dry fly or woolly worm
tackle.technique: Use a small bobber, 18-inch leader, small hook, small bait. Fish near structure (docks, weeds, brush). Let the bobber do the watching. Simple and effective — ideal for kids.

funFacts: Bluegill can detect ultraviolet light that humans cannot see
A large female can deposit up to 60,000 eggs
Bluegill are the most popular panfish in America — more bluegill are caught than any other species
baseline.memoryHook: BLUE-gill = BLUE ear flap (opercular flap). Classic bobber-and-worm panfish. Vertical bars, orange belly.

baseline.name: Black Crappie
baseline.description: Silver-black speckled fish with 7-8 dorsal spines. No distinct dark patch on the cheek (unlike white crappie). School heavily around submerged structure. One of the best-tasting panfish.
baseline.season: Year-round. Best spring (spawning April-June) and fall.
gpsHints: Sunset Lake — boat ramp off Sunset Beach Ln. Fish submerged timber and dock areas
baseline.regulations: 25 per day, no size limit in Oregon.

tackle.technique: Fish near submerged brush piles and dock pilings. Vertical jigging works well. Float with live minnow just above structure. Crappie suspend at specific depths — move your bait until you find the right depth.

funFacts: Crappie are called "papermouth" because their mouths tear easily when hooked — be gentle!
They can detect food in near-zero visibility using their lateral line
A 15-inch crappie is a true trophy — most fish 8-12 inches
baseline.memoryHook: BLACK Crappie = speckled (irregular black spots), 7-8 dorsal spines, no cheek bar. PAPER-thin mouth — go easy!
identifyingFeatures: Silver base color with olive/dark markings

baseline.name: Brown Bullhead Catfish
baseline.description: Mottled brown catfish with 8 barbels (whiskers) around mouth. Sharp spines in pectoral and dorsal fins — handle carefully! Squared or slightly notched tail. Excellent eating when from clean water.
baseline.season: Spring through fall. Peak May-September. Night fishing in summer is best.
gpsHints: Coffenbury Lake — fish the muddy bottom in the deeper northern section after dark in summer
baseline.regulations: No size or bag limit in Oregon for bullhead catfish.

tackle.technique: Fish on the bottom with no float using a slip sinker rig. Set hook firmly when line starts moving — bullhead often mouth the bait. Night fishing in summer is most productive. Strong smell = better bait.

funFacts: Bullhead catfish can breathe air using a modified gill structure — surviving out of water briefly
They are extremely tolerant of low oxygen and warm, muddy water
Parent bullheads guard their young in a school, herding them with their mouths
baseline.memoryHook: BULLHEAD = mottled brown, SQUARED tail (vs. forked), 8 barbels. STINKY bait works best. Night fisher.
identifyingFeatures: Squared or slightly notched (not forked) tail
Sharp spines in pectoral and dorsal fins

bonus.name: Chum Salmon
bonus.description: Fourth most abundant Pacific salmon. Dark olive-green with distinctive purple blotchy vertical bars (especially in males). Calico-pattern coloring. Males develop large hooked jaw and large canine teeth — giving the "dog salmon" name.
bonus.season: Oct-Dec in Columbia River tributaries. Smaller run than Chinook/Coho.
gpsHints: Klaskanine River — hatchery on Klaskanine Hatchery Rd east of Astoria
bonus.regulations: Combined Angling Tag. Check ODFW — retention often limited. Some streams closed.

tackle.technique: Drift eggs or bright attractor flies/jigs. Chum can be selective — bright colors work. Not as commonly targeted as Chinook/Coho.

funFacts: The largest commercial Pacific salmon harvest globally
Their calico blotching intensifies dramatically as they approach spawning
Chum have the lowest fat content of all Pacific salmon — less prized for eating
bonus.memoryHook: CHUM = CALICO bars (purple blotches) + DOG teeth. FALL run, often overlooked.

bonus.name: Pink Salmon
bonus.description: Smallest Pacific salmon. In ocean: bright silver with large oval black spots on both tail lobes. Males develop large hump behind the head during spawning — giving the "humpback" nickname. ODD YEARS ONLY in Columbia (2027, 2029...).
bonus.season: Odd years only — Aug-Sept in Columbia River. Limited Clatsop County returns.
gpsHints: Columbia River near Astoria — check ODFW reports for odd-year returns before planning a trip
bonus.regulations: Combined Angling Tag. Odd years only. Check ODFW.

tackle.technique: Cast bright pink lures across current. Pink salmon hit spinners and spoons aggressively in saltwater; more sluggish in rivers.

funFacts: Pink salmon have the shortest life cycle of all Pacific salmon — exactly 2 years
Males grow a pronounced hump before spawning — unique among Pacific salmon
Their runs are so predictable (odd vs. even years) that fisheries managers can plan decades in advance
bonus.memoryHook: PINK = smallest salmon, HUMP on back (males), ODD years only, LARGE oval spots on BOTH tail lobes.
identifyingFeatures: Large oval black spots on both lobes of tail
Spawning males have large dorsal hump

bonus.name: Bull Trout
bonus.description: Native char with pale yellow, orange, and red spots on olive-green background. NO black spots. Requires the coldest, cleanest water of any Pacific Northwest fish — a canary-in-the-coalmine species. THREATENED — catch and release only.
bonus.season: Year-round in cold tributaries. Less active in warm summer months.
locations: Upper cold tributaries of Clatsop County streams
gpsHints: Access limited — upper Lewis & Clark River headwaters and protected wilderness tributaries
bonus.regulations: THREATENED SPECIES. Catch-and-release only. Never retain. Use barbless hooks in their habitat.

tackle.reel: Fly reel or small spinning reel
tackle.technique: Cold, clear upper tributaries. Use light gear and barbless hooks. Handle very carefully — wet hands. Treat every bull trout like the treasure it is.

funFacts: Bull trout require water below 55°F to survive — they cannot live in degraded or warm streams
Their presence indicates excellent water quality and healthy forests
Bull trout were extirpated from many drainages due to dam construction and stream warming
bonus.memoryHook: BULL trout = colored spots (orange/red/yellow), NO black spots. COLD water only. THREATENED — always release!
identifyingFeatures: Orange, yellow, and red spots on olive body

bonus.name: Pacific Lamprey
bonus.description: Ancient, eel-like jawless fish with a sucker disc instead of a jaw. Dark grey-blue, smooth skin, no scales. Culturally and spiritually significant to Columbia River Tribes who have harvested them for thousands of years. Not commonly targeted by sport anglers.
bonus.season: Adult migration: March-July upriver. Larvae (ammocoetes) in stream sediments for 3-7 years.
gpsHints: Tribal harvest occurs at traditional locations — do not interfere with tribal fishing activities
bonus.regulations: Sport harvest regulated — check ODFW. Significant tribal cultural rights apply. Do not interfere with tribal harvest.

lures: Not typically targeted by sport anglers
tackle.technique: Not commonly targeted. If incidentally caught, handle gently and release carefully.

funFacts: Pacific lamprey have been used by Columbia River tribes for food, medicine, and trade for over 10,000 years
Larvae spend up to 7 years buried in stream sediment before metamorphosing into adults
They lack jaws entirely — their circular sucker disc is ringed with teeth for parasitic feeding at sea
bonus.memoryHook: LAMPREY = eel-like, SUCKER DISC mouth, no jaw, no scales. Ancient fish. Culturally vital to tribes.
identifyingFeatures: Circular sucker disc with teeth instead of jaw
Eel-like body with no paired fins
7 circular gill openings on each side

bonus.name: Eulachon
bonus.description: Tiny, extremely oily smelt-like fish historically so important that coastal tribes rendered their fat for trade. So oily a dried eulachon can be lit and burned like a candle — hence "candlefish." Runs in lower Columbia River in spring via dip-net.
bonus.season: Feb-April in lower Columbia River. Large schools detectable in clear water.
gpsHints: Lower Columbia River — Tongue Point area and estuary. Dip-netting from boats during runs.
bonus.regulations: Dip-net license and Columbia River endorsement required. Check ODFW for specific seasons — harvest has been restricted in recent years due to population concerns.

tackle.technique: Dip-net from boat in lower Columbia during spring runs. Traditional harvest method. Eulachon are so small they pass through most hook-and-line tackle.

funFacts: Eulachon grease was such an important trade commodity that trade routes were called "grease trails"
They are so oily that a dried, cured eulachon can be lit and will burn steadily like a candle
Their Columbia River run has declined significantly — now a Species of Concern
bonus.memoryHook: EULACHON = CANDLEFISH. So oily it burns. TINY, runs in Feb-Apr. DIP NET only. "Grease trail" trade fish.

bonus.name: Northern Pikeminnow
bonus.description: Native predatory minnow — large, torpedo-shaped, olive-brown. Responsible for consuming millions of juvenile salmon per year near Columbia River dams. A BOUNTY PROGRAM pays $8-10+ per fish reported and you can collect at ODFW checkpoints.
bonus.season: Year-round. Best May-Sept when water is warm.
gpsHints: Columbia River — can be caught throughout. Bonneville area most famous for the bounty fishery.
bonus.regulations: BOUNTY PROGRAM: Register with ODFW, collect $8-10+ per fish (over 9 inches). Paid daily at check stations. No bag limit. Encouraged harvest!

tackle.technique: Cast near current seams in the Columbia. Pike minnow are aggressive — they'll hit spinners readily. Bring them to ODFW check stations same day for bounty payment.

funFacts: The bounty program (since 1990) has paid out millions of dollars and removed tens of millions of pikeminnow from the Columbia
Each pikeminnow eats an estimated 1 juvenile salmon per day near dams
The bounty increases to $10+ for larger fish
bonus.memoryHook: PIKEMINNOW = BOUNTY fish! $8-10 per fish. Olive torpedo. Columbia River salmon predator. GET PAID to fish.
identifyingFeatures: Large mouth for a minnow, terminal (front-facing)

bonus.name: Largescale Sucker
bonus.description: Native bottom-feeding fish with distinctive downward-facing sucker mouth. Olive-brown with large scales. Frequently caught by trout anglers using worms. Not targeted but quite common. Often mistaken for carp or suckers from other regions.
bonus.season: Year-round. Spawning March-June in gravel streams.
gpsHints: Columbia River tributaries — especially during spring spawning runs in gravel-bed streams
bonus.regulations: No bag limit or size limit. Considered an incidental catch species.

tackle.technique: Not typically targeted. Most often caught incidentally while fishing for trout. Found in all types of flowing water from small creeks to large rivers.

funFacts: Suckers play an important ecological role — their bottom-feeding stirs up invertebrates for other fish
Their sucker mouth can extend downward to vacuum food from rocks and gravel
They are a very old fish family — related to fish that existed 50 million years ago
bonus.memoryHook: SUCKER = DOWNWARD-facing sucker mouth, large scales, olive-brown. Often caught by accident on worms.
identifyingFeatures: Sucker-type downward-facing mouth with thick, fleshy lips

bonus.name: Starry Flounder
bonus.description: Flatfish of the estuary and bay. Distinguished from other flounders by its alternating dark and light bands on the dorsal and anal fins — like yellow and black barber stripes. Eyes can be on either side (right or left). Found in muddy estuaries.
bonus.season: Year-round in estuaries. Best Sept-April.
gpsHints: Youngs Bay — fish muddy bottom areas near the mouth. Access from Astoria waterfront.
bonus.regulations: 5 per day, 12-inch minimum. Check ODFW.

tackle.technique: Fish on the muddy bottom of estuaries with natural bait. Slow, patient fishing. Look for muddy/sandy flats in Youngs Bay and Columbia estuary channels.

funFacts: Starry flounder can have eyes on either the left or right side — unlike most flatfish which are consistently one or the other
Their distinctive fin stripes make them easy to identify
They are a popular target for kids fishing from piers and docks in Astoria
bonus.memoryHook: STARRY flounder = STRIPED fins (yellow/black bands), can be EITHER side (left or right-eyed). Estuary flatfish.
identifyingFeatures: Alternating yellow and dark bands on dorsal and anal fins
Eyes on either left or right side (variable)

bonus.name: Spiny Dogfish
bonus.description: Small shark with a sharp spine in front of each dorsal fin — be careful when handling! Slate-gray with white spots. Often caught incidentally while bottomfishing. Surprisingly good eating — very popular in British fish-and-chips.
bonus.season: Year-round, common spring and fall when schools move through.
gpsHints: Any nearshore bottomfishing area — often caught mixed in with rockfish and lingcod
bonus.regulations: Check ODFW. Historically not heavily regulated but check current rules. Good eating if prepared correctly.

lures: Any fresh bait on the bottom
tackle.technique: Usually caught incidentally while bottomfishing for rockfish or lingcod. Spiny dogfish travel in large schools — if you catch one, you'll often catch many.

funFacts: Spiny dogfish are the most abundant shark in the world
They have one of the longest pregnancies of any vertebrate — 22-24 months
The spine in front of each dorsal fin can inject a mild venom — handle carefully
bonus.memoryHook: SPINY dogfish = SPINE in front of each dorsal fin. Small shark. VENOMOUS spines — handle carefully!
identifyingFeatures: Sharp spine in front of each dorsal fin

bonus.name: Kelp Greenling
bonus.description: Beautiful reef fish where males and females look COMPLETELY different. Males: gray-blue with irregular orange-brown spots. Females: tan to reddish-brown with rounded dark spots. Found in kelp beds and rocky reefs. Excellent eating.
bonus.season: Year-round but best May-October.
locations: Rocky reefs and kelp beds off Cannon Beach and Tillamook Head
gpsHints: Tillamook Head nearshore reefs — boat access, 30-80ft depth
bonus.regulations: 5 per day (check ODFW — part of greenling aggregate limit).

lures: Bare hook with bait (shrimp or herring)
tackle.technique: Fish near kelp and rocky structure. Cast into kelp beds and work jig slowly. Kelp greenling are inquisitive and will investigate anything that looks like food.

funFacts: Male and female kelp greenling look so different they were once classified as separate species
They are year-round residents of kelp forest ecosystems, unlike migratory salmon
Their flesh is considered superior table fare — mild and firm
bonus.memoryHook: KELP greenling = males and females look TOTALLY DIFFERENT. Males: blue-gray + orange spots. Females: reddish + dark spots.
identifyingFeatures: Males: blue-gray with irregular orange-brown spots
Females: tan/reddish with dark rounded spots
Long dorsal fin running most of body

bonus.name: Pacific Cod
bonus.description: Classic "true" cod with pale brown-gray mottled body, three distinct dorsal fins, barbel on chin, and white lateral line. Excellent table fare. Found in deeper water than most nearshore species — typically 100-900 feet.
bonus.season: Best fall and winter when they move shallower. Year-round in deeper water.
locations: Charter boats from Warrenton targeting deeper water
gpsHints: Offshore deeper water (100-300ft) west of Tillamook Head — charter boat territory
bonus.regulations: 10 per day (check ODFW). Part of groundfish complex regulations.

lures: Whole herring or squid on bottom
tackle.technique: Fish on bottom in deeper water. Heavy jigs dropped to the seafloor and jigged vertically. Pacific cod school near the bottom — once you find them, it can be fast action.

funFacts: Pacific cod can live up to 18 years
They were a critical food source for indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest for thousands of years
Pacific cod have three dorsal fins and two anal fins — unusual among fish
bonus.memoryHook: PACIFIC COD = THREE dorsal fins, chin barbel, white lateral line. DEEPER water. Classic fish-and-chips fish.
identifyingFeatures: White lateral line on brownish body

bonus.name: Pacific Sanddab
bonus.description: Small, left-eyed flatfish found in sandy and muddy bottoms. Light brown with orange-brown mottling. Eyes are on the LEFT side (unlike most flatfish). One of the most delicious small fish in the Pacific — prized by chefs.
bonus.season: Year-round but most common summer and fall in shallower water.
locations: Mixed catches with rockfish and lingcod
gpsHints: Sandy bottom areas offshore — often caught mixed in with other bottomfish species
bonus.regulations: Check ODFW groundfish regulations. Typically generous bag limits.

tackle.reel: Any appropriate spinning or conventional reel
tackle.technique: Fish on sandy/muddy bottom. Usually caught in mixed catches while targeting other species. Light gear if targeting specifically. They're small — maximize by using small hooks.

funFacts: Pacific sanddab are considered one of the most delicious fish in the Pacific — prized in San Francisco restaurants
They are left-eyed flatfish — both eyes end up on the left side as they develop
Sanddab can change their color pattern to match the seafloor precisely
bonus.memoryHook: SANDDAB = LEFT-eyed flatfish, small, sandy-brown. Delicious tiny flatfish. LEFT eyes (remember: sanddab = sinister = left).
identifyingFeatures: Both eyes on LEFT side of body

bonus.name: Striped Bass
bonus.description: Large, powerful fish with 7-8 distinct horizontal stripes running from gill to tail. Introduced to Pacific Coast from East Coast in 1879. Occasional strays near Columbia River mouth and Tillamook Bay. Silver with olive-green back.
bonus.season: Summer-fall. Occasional catches near Columbia mouth June-October.
gpsHints: Columbia River mouth area — near jetties. Very opportunistic catches — rare in Clatsop County.
bonus.regulations: Check ODFW. 2 per day, minimum 18 inches in Oregon. Regulations may change — verify.

tackle.technique: Cast large lures near structure in tidal areas. Stripers ambush baitfish at tidal transitions. Fish incoming tides near jetty rocks.

funFacts: Striped bass were introduced to San Francisco Bay in 1879 and spread up the coast
They can live over 30 years and grow to 80+ lbs
Stripers are anadromous — they live in salt water but spawn in freshwater rivers
bonus.memoryHook: STRIPER = 7-8 HORIZONTAL STRIPES head-to-tail. Silver + olive. Introduced from East Coast. RARE here.

bonus.name: Pile Perch
bonus.description: Largest of Oregon's surfperch family. Silver with a distinctive dark blotch at the base of the pectoral fin. Found around dock pilings, jetty rocks, and pier structures in Astoria and Warrenton. Good eating.
bonus.season: Year-round near pilings. Best May-October.
gpsHints: Astoria waterfront — fish the pilings along the bay waterfront. Easy bank access.
Warrenton docks — near the boat ramp area at the East Mooring Basin
bonus.regulations: 15 per day, no size limit.

tackle.technique: Fish right against the pilings. Mussels are the classic bait — scrape them off the pilings, smash slightly, put on hook. Simple and deadly. Fish on the bottom or mid-water near structure.

funFacts: Pile perch feed heavily on mussels — the bait literally comes from the same pilings you're fishing
They give live birth to 5-20 young per litter
Pile perch are one of the easiest fish to find in urban fishing areas — they live right under docks year-round
bonus.memoryHook: PILE perch = lives on PILINGS! Dark blotch on pectoral fin base. Use MUSSELS from the same pilings.
identifyingFeatures: Dark blotch at base of pectoral fin

bonus.name: Shiner Perch
bonus.description: Tiny but beautiful perch of the estuary. Shiny silver with 3 yellow bars on the sides and a distinctive yellow blotch at the base of the dorsal fin. Extremely common around docks in Astoria. Often caught by children.
bonus.season: Year-round in estuaries and bays.
gpsHints: Any dock or pier along the Astoria waterfront — shiner perch are extremely abundant
bonus.regulations: No bag or size limit.

tackle.technique: Drop bait right off the dock edge. No casting needed — shiner perch are right below you. Perfect beginner and kids' fish. Very easy to catch.

funFacts: Shiner perch are viviparous — giving birth to live young
A single dock can harbor hundreds of shiner perch
They are an important food source for larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals
bonus.memoryHook: SHINER perch = 3 yellow bars, yellow dorsal blotch. Tiny. Under EVERY dock. Perfect kids' fish.
identifyingFeatures: Yellow blotch at base of dorsal fin

bonus.name: Pacific Staghorn Sculpin
bonus.description: Bizarre-looking estuary sculpin with large, flat head and antler-like preopercular spines (deer antler appearance). Brown-olive mottled coloring. Extremely common in mudflats and estuaries. Often caught accidentally. Excellent live bait for larger fish.
bonus.season: Year-round in estuaries. Most active at low tide on mudflats.
locations: Fort Stevens state park nearshore areas
gpsHints: Youngs Bay mudflats — accessible from various pullouts along Hwy 101 south of Astoria
bonus.regulations: No bag limit or size limit. Often used as baitfish.

tackle.technique: Usually caught accidentally while fishing estuaries. If targeting for bait: use small hook with worm on the mudflat bottom. Handle with care — preopercular spines are sharp!

funFacts: The staghorn sculpin can survive in water with very low oxygen by using its modified gill structure to breathe air
Their remarkable camouflage makes them nearly invisible on estuary mudflats
They are an important prey species for herons, seals, and larger fish in the estuary
bonus.memoryHook: STAGHORN sculpin = ANTLER-like spines on head (preopercular). Estuary mudflat. Mottled brown. Excellent BAITFISH.
identifyingFeatures: Large, flat head with branched antler-like preopercular spines

bonus.name: Peamouth Chub
bonus.description: Native minnow of Pacific Northwest lakes and rivers. Olive-brown with 2-3 pale stripes along the sides. Develops red coloring on mouth and sides during spawning season. Often mistaken for other minnow species. Common in Clatsop County lakes.
bonus.season: Year-round. Spawning April-June when red coloring is most visible.
gpsHints: Cullaby Lake — found throughout, often in shallow weedy areas
bonus.regulations: No bag limit or size limit. Not commonly targeted.

tackle.technique: Small hooks and tiny baits. Usually caught accidentally while targeting perch or crappie. Abundant in local lakes.

funFacts: Peamouth is one of the most common native fish in Oregon lakes and is rarely recognized by anglers
During spawning, males develop vivid red coloring and look completely different from non-spawning fish
They form large schools in open water during summer
bonus.memoryHook: PEAMOUTH = native minnow, 2 pale stripes, turns RED around mouth when spawning. Common, rarely recognized.
identifyingFeatures: 2-3 pale lateral stripes on olive body
Red coloring around mouth during spawning

bonus.name: Pumpkinseed
bonus.description: Perhaps the most colorful freshwater fish in Oregon. Blue-green with orange and red spots, orange-red belly, blue cheek markings, and a distinctive red or orange edge on the black ear flap (opercular flap). Found in warmer Clatsop County lakes.
bonus.season: Year-round but best April-September. Spawning May-July.
gpsHints: Cullaby Lake — weed beds along the eastern shore
bonus.regulations: 25 per day, no size limit.

tackle.technique: Fish near shallow weed beds with bobber and worm. Pumpkinseed are not picky — they'll hit almost anything small. Great kids' fish.

funFacts: Pumpkinseed are one of the most elaborately colored freshwater fish in North America
They can crush snails with specialized pharyngeal (throat) teeth — a diet niche no other sunfish exploits
They hybridize readily with bluegill where the two species overlap
bonus.memoryHook: PUMPKINSEED = orange-and-blue PUMPKIN colors, red edge on the ear flap. Most COLORFUL local sunfish.
identifyingFeatures: Red or orange edge on black ear flap (opercular flap)

bonus.name: White Crappie
bonus.description: Similar to Black Crappie but paler silver-white with distinct vertical bars (not irregular spots). KEY ID: White Crappie has 5-6 dorsal spines (vs. 7-8 for Black Crappie). Bars vs. spots is the easiest field mark. Excellent eating.
bonus.season: Year-round. Best spring (spawning April-June) and fall.
gpsHints: Sunset Lake — submerged brush piles and docks. Launch from Sunset Beach Ln boat ramp.
bonus.regulations: 25 per day, no size limit.

tackle.technique: Identical to black crappie fishing — vertical jigging near structure or float with live minnow. White crappie often prefer slightly deeper, more open water than black crappie.

funFacts: White crappie are more tolerant of turbid (murky) water than black crappie — this helps separate their habitat preferences
They can live in schools of thousands during winter, suspended at a specific depth
A white crappie's 5-6 dorsal spines vs. black crappie's 7-8 is the most reliable way to tell them apart
bonus.memoryHook: WHITE crappie = VERTICAL BARS (not spots), 5-6 dorsal spines (vs. black crappie's 7-8). Paler color.
identifyingFeatures: Distinct vertical bars (not irregular spots like black crappie)
5-6 spines in dorsal fin (fewer than black crappie)
Slightly longer body, more elongated than black crappie

bonus.name: Tench
bonus.description: Rare introduced European species found in Coffenbury Lake (Fort Stevens). Stocky, olive-green with tiny scales, very small rounded fins, and tiny barbels at corners of mouth. Mucus-covered. Rarely caught — most anglers have never seen one.
bonus.season: Year-round. Most active July-September in warm water.
locations: Coffenbury Lake (Fort Stevens State Park) — primary location
gpsHints: Coffenbury Lake — parking off Ridge Road in Fort Stevens State Park. Fish the southern weedy areas.
bonus.regulations: No specific regulations. Not commonly encountered.

lures: Sweet corn on small hook (traditional European method)
tackle.technique: Fish the bottom of weedy, warm areas of Coffenbury Lake with natural bait. Very difficult to target specifically. Slow, patient fishing in late summer. If you catch one, it's a genuine trophy catch.

funFacts: Tench secrete a mucus thought to have healing properties — medieval physicians believed other fish would rub against tench to cure themselves, hence "doctor fish"
They are extremely rare in Oregon — Coffenbury Lake is one of very few known populations
Tench can survive low-oxygen conditions that would kill most fish by gulping air at the surface
bonus.memoryHook: TENCH = olive-green, slimy, TINY barbels, TINY scales. European import. Coffenbury Lake ONLY. Very rare catch.
identifyingFeatures: Tiny barbels at corners of mouth
Thick, stocky body with rounded fins
